new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Stress is dynamic (expiratory), word-level, and may fall on any syllable: marangó 'carpenter', discúrmu 'I rest', cúčubă 'log'. In the Farsherot dialect long vowels have been recorded (see 2.7.0). 2.1.3. In Aromanian the stressed and unstressed vowel systems differ considerably. In an unstressed syllable the height oppositions /e/ : /i/, /ă/ : /î/ and /o/ : /u/ are neutralised ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Free (lexical) dynamic word stress: no fixed position, illustrated with final (marangó), penultimate (discúrmu) and antepenultimate (cúčubă) stress; unstressed syllables show vowel-height neutralisation. Capidan 1932 §236 adds the diachronic view that stress normally stays on the syllable stressed in the Latin or loan etymon, with only minor shifts.
new_statements.exceptions: Narumov: none beyond Farsherot vowel length. Capidan 1932 §236 (pp. 371-373, saved file) lists sporadic shifts (curcubétă < cucúrbeta, misúr, Turkish/Greek/Slavic loans like sufră~sófră, vurcólac), morphological shifts (gen.-dat. pronouns a únei, verb class changes) and a syntactic one: with negation nu before vowel-initial verbs the stress moves to the negation (ascúltu but no-áscultu, adár but no-ádar).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('словесное') stress in citation forms; Capidan's no-áscultu case shows proclitic negation can attract stress in connected speech. Capidan §4 (p. 200) marks the accent only on words ending in a stressed vowel and on proparoxytones, i.e. paroxytones/consonant-final oxytones are the unmarked default in his transcription.
new_statements.identity_note: Narumov 2001 describes Aromanian as a whole ('арумынский язык/диалект', all dialect zones; arom1237), with dialect notes for Pindean, Gramoshtean, Farsherot (long vowels) and Moscopole varieties; Capidan 1932 likewise covers the whole dialect. No narrower variety/glottocode applies.

new_statements.quote: p. 222: « L'aroumain, comme le roumain et le grec, fait partie des langues à accent dynamique "à liberté limitée" où l'accent ne peut affecter qu'une zone limitée aux trois dernières syllabes d'une unité accentuelle. » — p. 223: « Dans ce cadre, la place de l'accent peut jouer un rôle intégré à la morphologie: sa place, sans échapper à la règle de la limitation syllabique, peut varier selon des règles morphologiques. ex: al'asu "je laisse" [...] - alas'əmu: "nous laissons" [...] En aroumain, la fonction de l'accent est distinctive, puisqu'il permet d'opposer par sa place différente des unités identiques du point de vue des phonèmes. » — p. 226-227: « Pourtant, si l'accent se place souvent à la pénultième et à l'antépénultième il n'affecte que rarement la syllabe finale. »
new_statements.translation: p. 222: 'Aromanian, like Romanian and Greek, belongs to the languages with a dynamic accent "of limited freedom", where the accent can affect only a zone restricted to the last three syllables of an accentual unit.' — p. 223: 'Within this frame, the place of the accent can play a role integrated into the morphology: its position, without escaping the rule of syllabic limitation, can vary according to morphological rules. e.g. al'asu "I leave" - alas'əmu "we leave" [...] In Aromanian, the function of the accent is distinctive, since by its different position it allows units identical in their phonemes to be opposed.' — pp. 226-227: 'However, while the accent is often placed on the penult and on the antepenult, it only rarely affects the final syllable.'
new_statements.citation: Béis, Stamatios. 2000. L'aroumain parlé à Metsovo: description d'une langue en voie de disparition. Thèse de doctorat, Université Paris V. 453 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with Narumov 2001 (existing statement: stress is dynamic, word-level, can fall on any syllable; lexical/unpredictable) and adds the constraint that the stress window is the last three syllables (antepenult, penult, final), that penult/antepenult are the normal positions and final stress marginal, that stress is contrastive but mostly through verbal morphology, and that clitics are unstressed and do not shift host stress. The catalog record for Aromanian has an empty rule field; Béis supplies a rule: free stress within a right-edge three-syllable window. Describes specifically the Metsovo (Greece) variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (intensity) stress, contrastive, free within a three-syllable window at the right edge of the accentual unit (antepenult, penult or final); the position is not phonologically predictable and can vary morphologically (al'asu ~ alas'əmu; d'oru ~ dor'ui; 'afla ~ afl'o). Penult and antepenult are the usual positions; final stress is rare and limited to (a) verb forms with always-stressed tense/person markers (avi'a, vidz'u), (b) Greek and Turkish loans stressed finally in the source language (sxuʎ'o, kafedz'i, luγariasm'o), (c) indefinite-pronoun compounds (tsinev'a, tsiv'a, altsiv'a). Enclitics (definite article, possessives, personal pronouns) and proclitics (prepositions, mood markers, relative tsi, copula i) are unstressed and do not shift the stress of the host (fr'ateɲi, k'artea); vowel syncope in the host sometimes preserves an antepenultimate pattern (kl'oputulu > [kl'optulu]). Stressed vowels are louder, higher and sometimes slightly lengthened; mid/close vowel oppositions neutralise in unstressed syllables. Accentual unit = stretch with a single main dynamic accent, usually the traditional word; clitic groups behave as prosodic words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the accentual unit is defined as a sequence 'with a single main dynamic accent' (p. 224). Author notes that units cannot contain more than two unstressed syllables after the stressed one and rarely exceed five syllables (p. 223).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress is 'rare' and 'of no distinctive value' as a pattern but occurs in: verb forms with always-stressed modality/person amalgams (imperfect avi'a, passé limité vidz'u); Greek/Turkish loans with source-language final stress (sxuʎ'o 'school', kafedz'i 'café keeper', luγariasm'o 'bill'); indefinite-pronoun synthemes (tsinev'a, tsiv'a, altsiv'a). Clitics never take the accent. Minimal pairs by stress position are few and mostly verbal ('afla 'he finds' ~ afl'o 'he found').
new_statements.identity_note: Béis 2000 describes the Aromanian of Metsovo (Métsovo, Epirus, north-western Greece), a Pindus variety, from fieldwork recordings; the prosody chapter frames the statements as holding for Aromanian generally ('L'aroumain, comme le roumain et le grec..'), with corpus-specific remarks (rare final stress) drawn from the Metsovo corpus. Narumov 2001 (existing statement) is a general description of Aromanian with a note on the Farsherot dialect for long vowels.
